title: The arrow in the dark
hookLine: Dasharatha dies of grief, and an arrow from his youth comes home: karma
last: SEVA: SERVING IS A WAY TO LOVE GOD.

cards: The charioteer who drove Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to the edge of the kingdom comes back alone. The chariot is empty. Dasharatha asks him to tell everything: what Rama said, how Sita looked, whether they were afraid.

At midnight, lying beside Queen Kausalya, the old king tells something he's never told anyone. As a young prince, he was proud of one skill: he could shoot an arrow at a sound, in the dark, and hit what he couldn't see.
One night by a river he heard what sounded like an elephant drinking. He shot. And a human voice cried out.

teach.b: It wasn't an elephant. It was a young man, a hermit's son, filling a water pot for his parents, who were old and blind. The arrow killed him.
Dasharatha carried the water, and the news, to the parents himself. The grieving father spoke a curse: you too will die grieving for your son.
Valmiki never names the young man; later tellings call him Shravan Kumar, and families still tell his story as a picture of a son who cares for his parents. Decades pass.
Then the curse arrives. Dasharatha tells Kausalya the whole story, and before morning he dies, grieving for Rama, for the crowning that never happened, for the boy by the river.
Here's the teaching under it, one of Hinduism's biggest: karma.
Karma means action, and every action bears fruit. Not a punishment handed down on the spot, but the way a seed becomes a tree: slowly, in its own time.
He never meant to kill anyone, but the arrow left the bow, and decades later its fruit came home.
Many Hindus read his death that way, as karma ripening; in Valmiki's telling, the king himself says a doer reaps what he has done. And karma isn't only a warning.
Good actions are seeds too: honesty, kindness, caring for your parents the way that young man did.

One more detail: tradition says the epic began when the poet Valmiki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of birds and heard its mate cry. His grief, in Sanskrit shoka, came out of him as the first verse, a shloka.

how: Many Hindus read Dasharatha's death as karma ripening, the fruit of an old action coming home; the story of the hermit's son (in later tradition Shravan Kumar) is still told to children as a picture of caring for parents.

o: a verse form used in old Sanskrit poems
grief, the deep sorrow that follows a loss
a curse spoken by someone who was wronged

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

Valmiki leaves him unnamed; the name comes from later tellings.
karma means instant punishment for every mistake
karma means every action bears fruit, often slowly. Dasharatha's arrow came home decades later.
tradition says the Ramayana began with a poet's grief
Valmiki's shoka, grief, became the first shloka.

games.q: you're young Dasharatha. you've shot at a sound in the dark and killed a hermit's son. his blind parents are waiting for water. what do you do?
o: leave quietly and tell no one.
carry the water to them and tell them yourself.
send a servant with the news.
games.why: he carries the water and the news himself. the grieving father curses him: you too will die grieving for a son. decades later, that fruit comes home.

practice: Think of one thing you did long ago that you'd take back if you could, or one kindness someone planted in you years ago that's still bearing fruit. Don't punish yourself; just see the seed and the tree.
If you pray, offer it to God and ask for help planting better seeds today. If not, choose one good action to plant before tonight.

wordCard.voice: Shoka: grief. A hermit's grief became a curse that came due decades later, and a poet's grief became the first verse of the Ramayana.

orig.note: Sanskrit: grief; tradition says Valmiki's shoka became the first shloka, a verse.

carryVoice: Your line: karma ripens, even decades later. A king learned it at midnight. See you tomorrow.
